Why the peak stays finite

Throughout, write r = 2/3 and s = 2/3 − ε, so that 1/3 ≤ s ≤ 2/3 and r − s = ε. Multiplying out xn+1 = Aεxn one coordinate at a time gives the recurrence

un+1 = (2/3)un + 6vn,   vn+1 = svn,   u0 = 0,   v0 = 1.

The second equation alone gives vn = sn, which is positive and never exceeds 1. Since u0 = 0 and every coefficient in the first equation is positive, every un is nonnegative as well. So the absolute values in Mn can be dropped: Mn = max(un, sn).

1. Diagonalizable exactly when ε > 0

The matrix is upper triangular, so its eigenvalues are the diagonal entries r = 2/3 and s = 2/3 − ε.

For ε > 0 these are distinct, and eigenvectors belonging to distinct eigenvalues are linearly independent, so two of them form a basis. Explicitly, Aε − rI has rows (0, 6) and (0, −ε), both of which force the second coordinate to vanish, so p1 = (1, 0). And Aε − sI has rows (ε, 6) and (0, 0), so the eigenvector equation is the single condition εx + 6y = 0, solved by p2 = (6, −ε). The matrix P with these columns has det P = −ε ≠ 0, and Aε = P diag(r, s) P−1.

At ε = 0 the single eigenvalue 2/3 has algebraic multiplicity 2, but A0 − (2/3)I has the lone nonzero entry 6 in its corner, so its null space is just the line through (1, 0). The geometric multiplicity is 1, less than 2: there is no basis of eigenvectors and A0 is not diagonalizable. (Another way to see it: a diagonalizable matrix whose only eigenvalue is 2/3 must equal P(2/3)IP−1 = (2/3)I, and A0 is not that.) The plot shows the two eigendirections swinging together as ε → 0 and merging exactly where the eigenbasis disappears.

2. Every orbit decays, but only after it grows

For ε > 0, write x0 = c1p1 + c2p2. The second coordinates give −εc2 = 1 and the first give c1 + 6c2 = 0, so c2 = −1/ε and c1 = 6/ε. Because Aεn multiplies each eigenvector by the nth power of its eigenvalue,

ε > 0:   un = 6(rn − sn)/ε,   vn = sn.

Both r and s lie strictly between 0 and 1, so rn and sn tend to 0, and so do both coordinates.

At ε = 0 there is no eigenbasis, but A0 = (2/3)I + N, where N has the single entry 6 and satisfies N2 = 0. Since I and N commute, the binomial theorem applies and every term beyond the first power of N vanishes: A0n = (2/3)nI + n(2/3)n−1N. Applied to (0, 1) this gives

ε = 0:   un = 6n(2/3)n−1,   vn = (2/3)n.

The factor n grows only linearly while (2/3)n−1 shrinks geometrically, so this orbit tends to the origin too. In fact the two formulas are one formula. Dividing rn − sn by r − s = ε gives

un = 6(rn−1 + rn−2s + ⋯ + sn−1),

a sum of n terms that makes sense for every ε and collapses to 6nrn−1 when s = r. The defective case is the continuous limit of the diagonalizable ones.

Decay does not begin at once. The recurrence gives u1 = 6v0 = 6 for every ε, so M0 = 1 and M1 = 6: the size is multiplied by 6 in a single step even though both eigenvalues are smaller than 1. Eigenvalues govern the long run; the first step is governed by the off-diagonal entry 6, which pours the second coordinate into the first before the damping takes hold.

3. The exact peak is 8 − 6ε, reached at n = 2

Since vn ≤ 1 while u1 = 6, the largest value of Mn is the largest value of un, and the iterations that attain it are exactly those where un is largest. From the recurrence,

u0 = 0,   u1 = 6,   u2 = 4 + 6s = 8 − 6ε,   u3 = (2/3)(8 − 6ε) + 6s2 = 8 − 12ε + 6ε2.

The consecutive differences are u1 − u0 = 6, then u2 − u1 = 2 − 6ε ≥ 0 (zero only at ε = 1/3), then u3 − u2 = −6ε(1 − ε) ≤ 0 (zero only at ε = 0).

Once the sequence stops rising it never rises again. Let dn = un+1 − un = −un/3 + 6sn. Substituting the recurrence into dn+1 and comparing with (2/3)dn gives

dn+1 = (2/3)dn − 6(1 − s)sn,

and the last term is strictly negative because 0 < s < 1. So whenever dn ≤ 0, the next difference dn+1 is strictly negative. Starting from d2 ≤ 0, induction gives u3 > u4 > u5 > ⋯. Altogether

u0 < u1 ≤ u2 ≥ u3 > u4 > u5 > ⋯,

so the maximum is u2: the exact peak is 8 − 6ε at n = 2. At ε = 1/3 the first inequality becomes an equality and the peak 6 is shared by n = 1 and n = 2. At ε = 0 the second becomes an equality and the peak 8 is shared by n = 2 and n = 3. For 0 < ε < 1/3 the peak is attained at n = 2 alone. Drag the ε slider to either end and the olive rings on the size graph mark the tie.

4. Nearly parallel eigenvectors, yet a bounded excursion

The eigenvectors (1, 0) and (6, −ε) make an angle whose tangent is ε/6, so they are nearly parallel over the whole parameter range and coincide at ε = 0. The coefficients c1 = 6/ε and c2 = −1/ε of x0 in that basis do blow up as ε → 0, and so does each of the two pieces 6rn/ε and 6sn/ε that make up un. That is what suggests unbounded growth.

But the two pieces are subtracted, and they nearly cancel. In the sum form of un above, each of the n terms is at most rn−1 because s ≤ r, so

un ≤ 6n(2/3)n−1 ≤ 6 · (4/3) = 8   for every ε and every n,

because n(2/3)n−1 is largest, equal to 4/3, at n = 2 and n = 3. (The same bound follows from the mean value theorem: rn − sn = nξn−1(r − s) for some ξ between s and r, so un = 6nξn−1 ≤ 6n(2/3)n−1.) Together with vn ≤ 1 this gives Mn ≤ 8 for all ε and all n. The peak 8 − 6ε rises toward 8 as ε → 0 and never exceeds it; the bound is attained at ε = 0.

What becomes unbounded as ε → 0 is the eigenvector matrix P and its inverse, not the orbit. Each xn = Aεnx0 is a polynomial in ε, so it depends continuously on ε and converges to the ε = 0 orbit, whose growth is a polynomial times a decaying exponential. The size of the transient is set by the entries of the matrix, the 6 and the 2/3, not by the angle between the eigenvectors.

Two lessons follow. Eigenvalues of absolute value less than 1 promise eventual decay but say nothing about how large the iterates get on the way; here they grow from 1 to 8. And a coalescing eigenbasis means the eigenvector coefficients become huge and misleading, not the vectors themselves. When the basis finally fails, the direct calculation with A0 = (2/3)I + N takes over and tells the same story.
